lessons.summary: Apply repeated doubling and exponential growth; multiplying and dividing powers with a common base; power of a power and powers of products through explained numerical problems.
objectives: Explain power play: guided examples and applications.
Calculate and interpret initial, stages, final using Qₖ = Q₀ × 2ᵏ.
Recognize why this claim fails: n doublings give Q₀+2n.

sections.heading: Retrieval before calculation
paragraphs: Qₙ=Q₀2ⁿ. The stage counter begins at zero with the starting amount. Adding 2 each stage makes linear growth, a different process. In a paper-folding model, the thickness formula is idealised: real paper cannot be folded arbitrarily many times. Conditions: The model assumes exact doubling at each stage; real physical constraints are separate.

bᵃbᶜ=bᵃ⁺ᶜ; bᵃ/bᶜ=bᵃ⁻ᶜ. b³ contains three copies of b. Multiplying by b⁴ contributes four more copies, giving seven altogether. Division cancels repeated copies, which also explains why a negative exponent is a reciprocal. Conditions: The quotient rule requires b≠0. The common-base condition is essential.

(bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ. The outer exponent repeats the entire inner block. For example, (2³)² contains two blocks of three copies of 2, giving six copies. A product is different from a sum: (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ but (a+b)ⁿ does not generally split. Conditions: Rules shown use integer powers; negative powers require nonzero factors.

sections.heading: Repeated doubling and exponential growth
paragraphs: Repeated doubling is multiplicative growth: each stage multiplies the current amount by 2. After n stages, the amount is Q₀2ⁿ.
Record the initial amount. Multiply by 2 once for each stage, or use 2ⁿ to combine the repeated factors. Check n=0 before interpreting the table so the first doubling is not counted twice.
Remember: Count multiplications, not additions.

sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing powers with a common base
paragraphs: For powers with the same nonzero base, multiplication adds exponents and division subtracts them.
Confirm the bases are equal before combining exponents. Use addition for multiplication and subtraction for division. Keep the order of the numerator and denominator; b²/b⁵=b⁻³, not b³.
Remember: Same base: multiply → add; divide → subtract.

sections.heading: Power of a power and powers of products
paragraphs: A power of a power multiplies exponents: (bᵃ)ᶜ=bᵃᶜ. Powers of a product distribute to each factor.

Identify the parentheses and the operation inside them. Multiply exponents for a powered power. Raise every factor in a product to the outer power. Check the expanded repeated multiplication for a small example.
Remember: Power of power: multiply counts. Product power: power every factor.

sections.heading: Review your errors
paragraphs: n doublings give Q₀+2n. Correction: That expression adds a fixed amount. Doubling uses the current total as the next multiplicand.
Add exponents when adding powers. Correction: 2²+2³=4+8=12, not 2⁵. The exponent rule applies to multiplication.
(a+b)²=a²+b². Correction: The cross term is missing. (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b².

Historical Mesopotamian separators and empty-place conventions varied, so a modern decimal digit display does not reproduce the ancient notation. Compare hours/minutes as a familiar grouping example.
A positional system gives a digit its value from both its symbol and its position. In base b the places are 1, b, b², b³ and so on.

sections.heading: Why the method works

Use a separate landmark symbol for each value; repetition supplies its count.

practice.hint: Start from N = Σ symbol count × landmark. Decompose the value into landmark multiples.

formulas.meaning: The position of a symbol can affect whether it adds or forms a subtractive pair, but it is not a general power-of-ten place-value digit. Modern conventional Roman notation has no zero digit and does not represent every signed or decimal number.
formulas.restriction: Modern conventional form; integers 1–3999 only. Historical usage was not always uniform.

formulas.meaning: This example helps distinguish an additive system from a positional one. Ten units can be exchanged for one ten-symbol, but moving a one-symbol to another place does not by itself turn it into a hundred. The tool displays symbol counts rather than reproducing ancient glyphs.
formulas.restriction: Illustrates powers-of-ten additive representation through 99999; historical glyph forms are not simulated.

formulas.meaning: Only digits 0 through b−1 are allowed. A zero digit holds an empty place: 101 in base 2 means one four, zero twos and one unit. Without its position, a digit alone cannot tell the full contribution.
formulas.restriction: This tool uses ordinary integer bases 2–36. Letters A–Z represent digits 10–35; historical exceptions require their own model.

misconceptions.mistake: Any small symbol can be subtracted from any larger symbol.
misconceptions.correction: The conventional form permits particular pairs. For 49 use XLIX, not IL.

misconceptions.mistake: A ten-symbol becomes a hundred-symbol when moved left.
misconceptions.correction: In an additive system its designated value stays the same. A positional system works differently.

misconceptions.mistake: Every numeral system uses exactly the same place weights.
misconceptions.correction: Egyptian additive notation and calendar-style Mayan weights illustrate why the convention must be stated.
